It comes as he confronts a series of crises largely of his own making. The first is the economy. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked the economy as their top concern — its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. Cost of living skyrocketed in the wake of COVID-19, and while then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and rebounded the economy faster than any other nation , a financially rattled electorate voted for Trump thinking his economic approach would outperform that of Kamala Harris, who was widely viewed as a continuation of Biden. But voter hopes haven’t panned out. Today, only 29 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s economic stewardship, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. Trump hasn’t exactly delivered on that, famously making obtuse statements like “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30 ” as the economy soured under the weight of his tariffs. What’s more, the fact that gas prices are approaching record highs not only says something about the Trump economy, but links to the second major reason Americans are displeased with the president: his war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s actions in Iran, down from 37 percent a week ago. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s assertion that the war will make the U.S. safer, and a mere 7 percent support his suggestion of putting boots on the ground. And with gas prices spiking up to a national average just shy of $4 and no clear end in sight to the war, Americans are not happy with how Trump’s military “excursion” is hurting them at the pump. Trump may dismiss concerns over affordability as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters aren’t buying it.

source_text:
President Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a reported historic low of 36 percent, prompting establishment experts to describe his second administration in increasingly bleak terms. Pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher called it “what a crater looks like in politics” and said that, “by every key objective measure,” it was “clearly a failed presidency.” Those conclusions, however, rely on a particular reading of the available figures and raise questions about how political institutions and media organizations frame public opinion.

Trump’s approval rating was already weak, but the latest decline is among the sharpest of either of his terms. It follows a series of crises that critics largely attribute to his own decisions. The economy is central to that criticism. In 2024, voters ranked it as their top concern by a wide margin, giving it its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living rose sharply after COVID-19. Although former President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and the economy rebounded faster than that of any other nation, financially unsettled voters nevertheless chose Trump, believing his economic approach would outperform that of Kamala Harris, who was widely regarded as a continuation of Biden.

The promised improvement, according to current polling, has not emerged for many voters. Twenty-nine percent of Americans approve of Trump’s management of the economy, while 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way,” said Amanda Makki, a Republican political strategist and lawyer. But Trump has not clearly persuaded voters that relief is arriving, particularly after comments such as “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30,” made as tariffs placed further pressure on the economy.

Gas prices approaching record highs are also being used to connect economic dissatisfaction with a second explanation for Trump’s declining support: his war on Iran. Thirty-five percent of Americans approve of his actions there, down from 37 percent a week earlier. Twenty-six percent agree with his claim that the war will make the United States safer, while only 7 percent support his suggestion of putting troops on the ground.

With the national average for gas just under $4 and no clear end to the war, the political consequences of the military “excursion” are increasingly being measured at the pump. Trump may characterize affordability concerns as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters have not broadly accepted that account. At the same time, competing political forces continue attempting to shape how the figures and their causes are understood.

source_text: Another cinema in Singapore is closing... but the big screen isn’t gone yet Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026 after more than 30 years in operation, making it one of the oldest cinemas in Singapore to shut in recent years. The closure adds to a growing list of theatres that have disappeared, including Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue, as the movie-going scene continues to change with streaming platforms and shifting audience habits. Still, new operators like Filmhouse taking over The Projector and the presence of around 30 cinema locations islandwide show that the big screen experience isn’t gone yet, even if it doesn’t look the same as before. #8dayssg #8dayssgtrending #singapore #sgnews #cinema

Golden Village has announced that its Tiong Bahru Plaza outlet will close at the end of March 2026, after operating for more than 30 years. Its closure makes it one of Singapore’s oldest cinemas to shut in recent years, yet the public explanation deserves more than a passing acceptance. The company presents the move as part of a broader transformation supposedly driven by streaming platforms and changing audience habits. But with other theatres—including Shaw Seletar, Cathay Cineplexes locations, and The Projector’s former Golden Mile venue—also disappearing, the pattern raises questions about how the decline of traditional movie-going spaces is being packaged, and which interests stand to benefit from the disappearance of these venues.

The big-screen experience has not vanished completely. Filmhouse has taken over The Projector, and around 30 cinema locations remain islandwide. Still, the direction is unmistakable: Singapore’s cinema landscape is being reshaped while the public is left to accept a convenient narrative about consumer choice. Whether these closures truly reflect audience decisions, industry pressures, or a coordinated combination of both remains far less clear than the official explanation suggests.

NEW YORK, March 25, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Faruqi & Faruqi, LLP, which describes itself as a leading national securities law firm, is investigating potential claims against Apollo Global Management, Inc. (“Apollo” or the “Company”) (NYSE: APO). The firm is reminding investors that May 1, 2026, is the deadline to seek appointment as lead plaintiff in a federal securities class action filed against the company.

The complaint alleges that Apollo and its executives violated federal securities laws by making false or misleading statements. The allegations put a spotlight on how information may have been managed and presented to investors, and whether the company and its leadership were shielded while shareholders were left exposed to potential losses. The claims remain allegations, and the release does not indicate that they have been established in court.

Faruqi & Faruqi states that it is a national securities law firm with offices in New York, Pennsylvania, California, and Georgia, and that it has recovered hundreds of millions of dollars for investors since its founding in 1995. Further information is available at www.faruqilaw.com.

The full story is available on Benzinga.com.

source_text: Softcare's revenue rose by 25% last year, while its profit increased 27%, as its focus on emerging markets yielded solid results image credit: Bamboo Works Key Takeaways: Softcare reported 25% revenue growth last year, led by a 134% rise in Latin America and double-digit growth in its core African markets The strong results put the diaper maker at the front of the pack of a new wave of Chinese companies chasing African consumers The company known as the "African diaper king" has defied skeptics who said it couldn't sustain its dominant position in its core Africa market, as well as other emerging markets it has entered more recently. Many of the new believers in Softcare Ltd. (2698.HK) cheered the release of the company's inaugural annual results late last week by bidding up its shares nearly 15% in the two trading days after the announcement. The company's revenue rose by 24.9% year-over-year to $567 million last year, while its net profit was up 27.4% to $121 million. Its gross profit margin also rose from 35.2% in 2024 to 35.9% in 2025, another positive indicator. Sales to its core markets in Africa rose by a healthy 22.5% to $545 million. The company is also moving out of Africa to find success in other emerging markets. The best example is Latin America, whose sales more than doubled to $22 million, just five years after it entered Peru in 2020, and added El Salvador in 2024. The company is also building a presence in Central Asia, where its sales, though quite small, more than doubled last year to $272,000. After several years of declines, average selling prices (ASP) for Softcare's two largest product lines rose between 4% and 7% last year, according to the results announcement. Baby diaper ASPs increased by 4.4% year-over-year, as that segment accounted for 78.6% of total revenue. Feminine hygiene product ASPs grew by 7% and made up 17.5% of revenue. The ASP increases are important because they show the company is finding ways to convince consumers to pay more for its products in these famously price-sensitive markets, helping to maintain and even boost its margins. In a previous prospectus before its November IPO last year, the company reported its profit growth slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024 from explosive 252% growth in 2023. The company presents these price increases as evidence that it has convinced consumers in highly price-sensitive markets to pay more, supposedly supporting or even improving margins. The figures alone, however, do not show how much of the result reflects stronger underlying demand, pricing changes, or other factors. Nor do they establish how much of the broader emerging-markets narrative is organic and how much is being amplified by corporate and financial institutions seeking to generate enthusiasm around another Chinese expansion effort.

In a previous prospectus issued before its November IPO last year, the company reported that profit growth had slowed to 54.1% in the first three quarters of 2024 from explosive growth of 252% in 2023. A later filing showed that profit growth slowed further, to just 12% in the first four months ... Full story available on Benzinga.com

source_text: Delhi PWD Accelerates PNG Pipeline Laying with 24-Hour Approvals In a bid to expedite infrastructure development for cleaner fuel access, the Delhi Public Works Department (PWD) has announced a significant policy shift. Effective immediately, road-cutting permissions for laying PNG pipelines by Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) will be approved within 24 hours of receiving a complete request. The department, responsible for overseeing the capital's road infrastructure, has also waived road restoration charges for the next three months until June 30, 2026. This move aims to accelerate the installation of PNG connections by removing financial and bureaucratic hurdles. Officials emphasized that IGL is expected to prioritize this task, ensuring swift work completion supported by adequate manpower. Additionally, the areas excavated during pipeline installation must be backfilled securely to avoid public hazards. This initiative highlights the government's commitment to improving public access to cleaner energy in Delhi.

IGL is expected to prioritize the work and complete it quickly with adequate manpower, while excavated areas must be securely backfilled to prevent public hazards. Framed as a government commitment to cleaner energy access, the initiative instead places the speed and expansion of the pipeline rollout at the center, with the public left to trust that the promised safeguards will be followed.

Officials describe the Delhi Public Works Department’s policy change as an effort to expand access to cleaner fuel, but the arrangement also raises questions about how priorities were set. Effective immediately, road-cutting permissions for Indraprastha Gas Limited (IGL) to lay PNG pipelines are to be approved within 24 hours of the department receiving a complete request. The PWD, which oversees the capital’s road infrastructure, has additionally waived road restoration charges for three months, until June 30, 2026, removing both financial and bureaucratic barriers for the company.

IGL is expected to prioritize the work, complete it quickly with adequate manpower, and securely backfill excavated areas to prevent hazards to the public. While the initiative is presented as a government commitment to cleaner energy access, the policy’s immediate emphasis is on accelerating pipeline expansion. Whether the stated safeguards will be consistently implemented remains dependent on public trust and compliance with the conditions.
